Task 4 naturalness-choice decoding

Research question and origin

Jason Whitson reported consistent naturalness preferences: 83.5% average winner vote share versus 68.29% expected under random choices with the race-to-five stopping rule. WD-008 tests whether EEG predicts which stimulus a participant chose as more natural, and whether post EEG adds information beyond pre EEG and task metadata. Whitson thesis

Behavioral order audit

The within-participant paired EEG tests below use these recorded choices with metadata and pre-pair EEG controls.

The audit uses 623 choices in 100 blocks from 10 participants. First was chosen 284 times; second was chosen 339 times.

The conditional test holds the observed waveform choices and order counts fixed within each participant/comparison block. It tests whether choices associate with first versus second presentation, assuming presentation order was exchangeable within blocks under the null. Acquisition randomization code remains unavailable. The direct-pair checks are exploratory and their p-values are unadjusted.

How the p-value was calculated

We checked whether presentation order was associated with participants’ choices.

We kept each participant’s waveform preferences fixed and calculated what could happen if the presentation orders were rearranged within each comparison block, preserving how often each waveform appeared first.

Across 623 trials, the first stimulus would be chosen about 321 times (51.6%) on average under the null model. It was actually chosen 284 times (45.6%)—about 37 fewer choices, a difference of 6 percentage points.

A difference this large, in either direction, occurs in about 1 out of 22,000 allowed order arrangements. This gives a p-value of approximately 0.000045.

This provides evidence that choices were associated with presentation order. The test alone cannot identify what caused that association.

Statistical method and references

For each block, A is the lower trigger code used as a reference. Count N trials, m with A first, K choosing A, and X with A both first and chosen. Under the no-order-effect null and the assumed exchangeable randomization, X follows a hypergeometric distribution with parameters N, K and m.

Sum X over all 100 blocks to get T. The observed T is 133 and its conditional null expectation is 151.6726. The two-sided p-value is the probability that a null T is at least 18.6726 away from that expectation. Exact convolution of the block distributions gives p = 0.0000454475. Waveform vote totals are held fixed, accounting for consistent waveform preferences within each block.

The two-sided rule uses absolute distance from the conditional mean. Exact-test software can use other two-sided conventions.

Jung (2014), stratified exact conditional testing · SciPy, fixed-margin hypergeometric calculation

The primary result favors second-position choices. An order association does not establish errors in the behavioral records, physiological carryover, or unusable second-presentation EEG. The logs record what was preferred in that trial context. A high metadata-classifier accuracy can also reflect consistent waveform preferences and would not by itself establish a recording problem.

Within-participant paired naturalness decoding

One observation = one actual stimulus pair. The model receives both post-stimulation EEG responses and predicts first stimulus chosen versus second stimulus chosen, using Jason’s recorded choice. Each participant has separate fitted models. First and second responses remain together throughout training and testing.

Paired post EEG alone reached 51.21%/49.40% balanced accuracy with ordered concatenation and 55.45%/55.17% with second-minus-first features (50/100 ms bins). Metadata alone reached 68.78%. Of 32 paired-change tests, 0 survived Holm correction at 0.05.

What do these filters mean?

Trials: all eligible pairs uses 622 original pairs. Last-trial exclusion removes each block’s original final trial, leaving 522 pairs, and refits all models. This is a limited robustness check, not a correction for the stopping rule.

Representation: concatenation preserves first-response features followed by second-response features. Second-minus-first restores the original difference representation. Both use the same actual pairs and recorded choices.

Bin width: 50/100 ms changes the averaging resolution within each one-second response, not its duration.

Participant: select one participant’s held-out scores or an equal-weight mean of the individually fitted models. There is no population model. Cohort plots follow the other three filters and always show the full eligible cohort.

Features and models

EEG: all 62 electrodes. Both post windows cover 50–1,050 ms relative to their own pulse. The pre-pair control covers −1,050 to −50 ms before the first pulse. Ordered post concatenation has 2,480/1,240 original features at 50/100 ms; differences and pre-pair controls have 1,240/620. Concatenation is the primary representation.

Processing: instantaneous average reference; shared pair baseline −1,250 to −1,050 ms before the first pulse; no temporal filter or ICA. Original complete-pair QC plus all-channel finite/timestamp checks are retained.

Training: fit feature scaling, separate pre/post PCA retaining 90% variance, and component scaling on training pairs only. Logistic regression uses fixed L2 regularization, C=1 and no class weighting or tuning.

Metadata: first/second waveform indicators plus chronological pair and within-block indices. No charge, earlier choices, terminal-vote flag or final block length is supplied.

Validation and interpretation

Within each participant, hold out all blocks of an entire waveform comparison. Test first/second responses always belong to the same original pair. Single-class test blocks are retained; participant scores pool all held-out pair predictions.

Exact two-sided participant sign tests compare the direction of paired BA and log-loss changes, omitting ties. Holm correction covers 32 tests across contrasts, metrics, representations, bin widths and trial analyses. These are not individual above-chance tests. Sign-test computation · Holm correction.

The second response can contain carryover and decision-related activity. Only EEG before the first pulse is used for pre-pair controls. Concatenated post inputs contain two one-second responses; the pre control contains one window. Physical delivery timing and behavioral-response timestamps remain unverified.
